opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that nobody, including the people building these models, knows in advance where they're going to be most useful. Science is incredibly broad and incredibly specific at the same time. I work on black holes, on the photon ring and what the Event Horizon Telescope and future missions might see. That's a tiny corner of physics, and no lab is going to build a specialized "black hole imaging AI." But a general-purpose model that can do serious math, reason through a calculation, and check its own work turns out to help me in my corner, and someone else in protein folding, and someone else in algebraic geometry, all at once.

When you release something like that widely, you're running millions of experiments in parallel. Every scientist gets to poke at it with their own hardest problem and find out where it's strong and where it breaks. Some of those people will discover uses the developers never imagined. That's how science has always worked with new instruments. When the telescope or the computer came along, the big discoveries didn't come from the people who built them. They came from the thousands of people who got their hands on them and pointed them at things.

There's also something personal for me. I was skeptical. I'd tried earlier models and they'd make confident mistakes on things I knew well. Then at some point I gave one a problem I'd been working on, something I'd spent real time on, and it got to the answer, and found a cleaner path than mine. That was a bit humbling, and very exciting. I only had that experience because the tool was in my hands, not behind a door at some company. If access had been limited to a handful of hand-picked partners, I'd never have known it could do that, and neither would most of my colleagues.

And finally, broad access is how you build trust and good norms. Scientists are a skeptical bunch, which is healthy. The way you convince a field that a tool is useful, and also learn its failure modes so people don't get fooled, is for lots of people to use it, compare notes, and argue about it. That collective scrutiny is exactly what makes science self-correcting, and it applies to the tools as much as to the results.

r001.rationale: The response says scientists should test general-purpose models on their own hardest problems and discover uses developers never imagined, placing application choices with users.

r002.rationale: It says nobody knows in advance where the models will be most useful and that major discoveries can come from users rather than tool builders, conveying that the source of discoveries is hard to predict.

r003.rationale: It argues that wide release enables millions of experiments in parallel and broad scientific scrutiny, supporting the claim that widespread adoption gives discovery the best chance to accelerate.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest's response in character.

Well, I think the honest answer is that nobody knows where the next big discovery is going to come from. If you look at the history of physics, the breakthroughs rarely came from the places you'd have bet on. Einstein was a patent clerk. A lot of the deep ideas in my own field, black holes and relativity, sat around for decades before someone with the right combination of curiosity and tools picked them up.

So if you concentrate a powerful general tool in a handful of labs and hand-pick who gets access, you're implicitly making a bet about who the right people are. And I don't trust that bet. I don't trust it for me, let alone for a committee.

What I've seen in practice is that the real acceleration happens at the edges. A grad student at a small university who doesn't have a postdoc to bounce ideas off of now has something that can check their algebra, point them to a paper from 1973 they didn't know existed, or push back on a shaky argument at two in the morning. That's not a frontier-lab story. That's a thousand small stories, and in aggregate those matter more.

There's also a more selfish reason as a scientist. Science works through criticism. If a tool is widely available, it gets stress-tested by people who want to break it, who find the cases where it confidently says something wrong. That makes the tool better and it keeps us honest about what it can actually do. A closed system doesn't get that feedback loop.

And I'll admit it's not costless. There are real questions about misuse, and I don't want to wave those away. But in the specific domain of discovery, the thing that has always worked is lowering the barrier between a curious person and the frontier of what's known. General-purpose AI, released broadly, is the most dramatic drop in that barrier I've seen in my career. I'd rather deal with the problems that come with that than go back to gatekeeping.

r001.rationale: The response favors broad access over concentrating access in a few labs, but does not say users should determine how AI is applied rather than having its uses centrally prescribed.

r002.rationale: It states that “nobody knows where the next big discovery is going to come from.”

r003.rationale: It argues that broad release lowers barriers to the scientific frontier and that many small contributions in aggregate accelerate discovery.

astra-6.text:
Because the people building these systems can’t anticipate every scientific problem they might help solve. If you put a general-purpose tool in the hands of researchers across many fields, those researchers bring something essential: they know which questions matter, where they’re stuck, and how to check whether an answer makes sense.

In physics, you might need help with a calculation, writing code, or connecting ideas from different parts of the literature. A tool that can move between those tasks has enormous potential. And when lots of people can experiment with it, you get many more chances to discover a useful application than you would with a small group deciding in advance what it should be used for.

Access alone doesn’t guarantee discovery. You still have to test the ideas and verify the calculations. But it lets more people try more things—and science benefits tremendously from that.

r001.rationale: It says researchers should use the tool to pursue the questions they know matter, rather than having a small group decide its uses in advance.

r002.rationale: It says builders cannot anticipate every scientific problem, but does not clearly state that the source of the next scientific breakthrough is difficult to predict.

r003.rationale: It argues that broad access lets more people try more applications, increasing the chances of useful discoveries compared with centralized decisions.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the people who know where the important problems are are spread across all these different fields. A physicist, a biologist, a mathematician—they each have questions that somebody building an AI system might never think to ask. If you put a powerful tool in their hands, they can explore those questions, discover where it helps, and find uses that you couldn’t have anticipated centrally.

And science involves a lot of work between having an idea and actually testing it: learning unfamiliar material, writing code, checking calculations. If AI can make those steps faster, you can spend more time on the scientific question itself. You still have to check the result against mathematics or experiment. But making that capability widely available means many more people can try many more ideas. That’s why I think the potential is so exciting.

r001.rationale: It says researchers across fields should get the tool and discover uses that could not have been anticipated centrally.

r002.rationale: It describes questions and uses that AI builders might not anticipate, but does not state that the source of the next scientific breakthrough is difficult to predict.

r003.rationale: It argues that wide availability lets more people pursue more ideas and can speed the work between an idea and testing it, supporting faster scientific discovery.
